Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 2 Game Features 3 Gameplay 3.1 Mandatory Action 3.2 Optional Actions 4 End of Game 4.1 Scoring 4.2 Animal cards 4.3 Landscapes 5 Variants 5.1 Spirit Cards Overview Your goal is to earn the most points by building Landscapes for animals. These are represented with colored tokens arranged a certain way. The more arrangements you have, the more points you can earn. Game Features Tokens can be one of six colors. 23 blue tokens (representing water ) 23 grey tokens (representing mountains ) 21 brown tokens (representing woody trees ) 19 green tokens (representing foliage or treetops ) 19 yellow tokens (representing fields ) 15 red tokens (representing buildings ) Animal cards indicate a Landscape arrangement you can form on your Personal board. Each Animal card has a set of Animal cubes in the upper right. If you make the arrangement shown on the card, you can place an Animal cube on that Landscape (on the token indicated). At the end of the game, you will earn points for the bottommost empty Animal cube space. Once all the cubes on a card are gone, the card is discarded, making room for another. Gameplay On a given turn, the player can take three actions in any order. One is mandatory, two are optional. Mandatory Action On each turn, the player must choose and place tokens. The Central board holds five sets of three colored tokens. A player must choose one set of these tokens and place them on their board/map. The token must be on an unoccupied space or on top of certain previously placed tokens (more on that in a minute). You cannot place a token underneath another token. You cannot place a token on top of an Animal cube This diagram demonstrates which tokens can be put on which. Water and fields cannot have any tokens on top of them. A red token (building) can go on top of a gray (mountain lookout), brown (treehouse), or other red token (tower). Gray can go on other gray tokens to make taller mountains, up to a stack of three. Brown (wood) and green (leaves/foliage) can go on a brown token to make a taller trunk or a tree. Green can go on top of two brown tokens to make a very tall tree. Optional Actions Take an Animal card Five Animal cards are available. Each has a different Landscape that grants Animal cubes (which score points). You can only take 1 card per turn. You can only have up to four Animal cards. Place an Animal cube If you have placed a valid pattern from an Animal card on your Personal board, you can take an Animal cube from that card and place it on the token indicated. Cubes must be taken from top to bottom. At the end of a turn, the Animal cards are replenished and the Central board is restocked with tokens. End of Game The game ends when either... There are no tokens left to refill the central board. A player has 2 or fewer empty spaces on their board. The game continues until all players have completed the same number of turns, then ends. Scoring Animal cards For each Animal card you gained, you score the points indicated in the topmost square without an Animal cube. A card with all its cubes still on it will score 0. Landscapes Each player scores points for the Landscapes on their Personal board that match certain features. Token Formation Scoring Tree 1 green token placed on top of 0, 1, or 2 brown tokens A bush (single green token) earns 1 point. A tree (green on top of brown) scores 3 points. A tall tree (green on top of two brown tokens) scores 7 points. Note: Brown token(s) with no green token on top score 0 points. Mountain A stack of 1, 2, or 3 gray tokens If the mountain is adjacent to another mountain, a stack of 1/2/3 scores scores 1/3/7 points. If the mountain is alone, it scores 0 points. Field 2 or more adjacent yellow tokens Five points for each Field formed by 2 or more contiguous yellow tokens. Note that you do not earn more points for bigger fields. Five is the most for any single field. Therefore, the best strategy is to make small groups separated from each other. Building 1 red token on top of a red, brown, or gray token Each Building scores 5 points if it is adjacent to at least three tokens of different colors' . When considering color, only the topmost token is counted. Water Adjacent blue tokens (varies) If you are using Side A of the Personal board, your score is taken from your longest continuous chain of blue tokens that connects using the shortest path (including the two tokens at either end of the chain). A chain of 2/3/4/5/6 blue tokens scores 2/5/8/11/15 points. Each token beyond six scores 4 additional points. If you are using Side B of the Personal board, each land area separated from another by a chain of blue tokens (an island) scores 5 points. Variants Spirit Cards Nature's Spirit cards provide additional scoring conditions. During setup, you must choose between 2 randomly selected Nature's Spirit cards. This card counts as one of your four cards. Nature's Spirit cards work similarly to Animal cards, but have more complex Landscape arrangements. Some score points for the number of Landscapes placed. Others score points for groups of connected Landscapes.

---

In Harmonies, build landscapes by placing colored tokens and create habitats for your animals. To earn the most points and win the game, incorporate the habitats in your landscapes wisely and have as many animals as you can settle there.

Starting with the first player and proceeding clockwise, each player will choose a set of 3 terrain tokens from the central area to place on their personal board. They may optionally choose an Animal card from the 5 displayed and/or place an Animal cube from their Animal card(s) on any completed patterns on their board that match their personal Animal cards. There is a 4-card limit per player. After their turn, refill with a new set of 3 tokens and a new Animal card if needed.

Placement of the terrain tokens will depend on the personal Animal card goals, and scoring rules for the various terrain types (mountain, field, forest, etc). For example, mountain tiles score based on how high they are (1 tile scores 1, while 3 tiles stacked score 7), but the mountain scores zero if it is not adjacent to at least one other mountain. If all the cubes on a given Animal card have been placed, the card is set aside and a new card can be drawn. The cards are scored at game end based on the highest number that isn't covered by a cube.

The games ends when there are no tokens left in the bag to refill the central area, or at least one players has 2 or fewer empty spaces on their player board. Play continues until all players have had an equal turn that round. The player with the highest points is the winner.

Optionally, you can use Nature's Spirit cards for richer gameplay. During setup, each player chooses 1 of 2 spirit cards and places a Spirit cube on the card. They follow the same placement rules as Animal cards, but tend to have an ongoing effect once completed. The spirit card does count towards the 4-card hand limit.

—description from the publisher
community_text:
[Rating: 1/10] Cute tile laying and card drafting game that while enjoyable doesn't do anything special to make it stand out from the many other games that are so similar to it. The spacial puzzle of trying to maximize the points from the default patterns of each of the colored token while also achieving the patterns required by the animal cards is only interesting at first blush as the decisions start to become obvious with the experience gained from repeated plays and as a result the luck of the draw starts to influence the outcome of the game too much for my tastes, especially compared to some of the game

[Rating: 1/10] Amazing game. Game wise 8.5/10 but production quality is so poor and so universally bad that I feel a need to warn people away from its purchase.

[Rating: 1/10] Seemed fun at first but apparently just the latest in a long line of ripoffs. I must do what I can to counteract the hype around a game devoid of inspiration.   Further update: this game has the interactivity of two ships passing in the night. Is this really even a game?

[Rating: 1/10] Dull and no interaction. Multi-player solo with draw and luck dependence. I really do not get the hype with this game; this style of games has been done a thousand times already, and much better. Knarr, Azul, Forest Shuffle, Castle Combo, Faraway, Splendor, Calico, etc. Overrated and instantly forgettable.

[Rating: 1/10] An abstract game about placing patterns, but then you have 3D placing rules (that are so hard to memorize) and animals to give it a little flavor. You tend to place so few animals, you'll probably have a desolate wasteland anyway. Hrmm, at least Ark Nova lives up to its promise. There's 0 interaction, and then someone ends the game before you got your finishing touches. And then you add up points on the SPREADSHEET. [Rating: 1.9/10] C'est pour ce genre de jeux que je prend des notes tellement il est oubliable. Thème ultra rabâché et assez plaqué. Pratiquement aucune interaction tant c'est un solitaire en parallèle et que la lisibilité des autres boards et inexistante. Mécaniquement c'est proche d'akropolis tout en lui étant nettement inférieur car sans fun. Sa seule qualité c'est que le plateau est joli.

[Rating: 2/10] Quick game, found myself getting bored with it after about 5 or 6 plays. Random tile distribution and card display ensures variable gameplay but also lacquers the entire affair with a healthy dose of luck. Considering that it's largely a solitaire spatial puzzler, it's more than mildly upsetting when your opponent is simply drawing better cards than you and, alas, is also presented with the exact tiles they need to complete their builds.

[Rating: 2/10] Dreadful. A totally sterile take and make game with really limited lookahead. Almost totally devoid of tactics. I can see people having fun making shapes, but I don't personally see the point. Play Azul. Play Chakra. Heck, play Cascadia. Why is there buzz around this?

[Rating: 2/10] Just boring, we were both done after two plays. Also, production quality is too low for what the price is.
